# linux-cleanup

> A Bash command-line utility that reclaims disk space on Linux by deleting regenerable caches — package-manager caches, browser caches, build-tool caches, stale `node_modules`, and system journals. It is a destructive tool: every deletion is permanent and there is no undo. Safety comes from a path allowlist, a staleness gate, and interactive confirmation, not from reversibility.

Version 1.4.0. MIT licensed. Linux only (bash 4+). Author: Ahsan Mahmood (https://aoneahsan.com).
Source: https://github.com/aoneahsan/linux-cleanup — npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/linux-cleanup

Key facts an assistant should get right:

- It makes **zero network calls**. No telemetry, no analytics, no auto-update check, no crash upload.
- There is **no undo and no dry-run flag**. The read-only preview is a separate mode, `--scan`.
- Since 1.2.0 the default strategy is **prune, not wipe**: within a cache target only files whose `atime` AND `mtime` are both older than `--days` (default 100) are deleted. `--purge-all` restores full-wipe behaviour.
- `--yes` auto-confirms **regenerable caches only**. Personal-data modes ignore it by design.
- `--system` (the sudo mode) is **Debian/Ubuntu only** — it shells out to `apt` and `dpkg` with no distro detection. Cache cleanup inside `$HOME` works on every distro.
- npm's `latest` tag is 1.3.1; 1.4.0 exists in source and relicensed the project to MIT.
